flags: The stated division of the vertex angle presumes that the altitude lies inside that angle.
The statement that the altitude divides the vertex angle is interpreted as an internal division; the complementary-angle argument requires that configuration.

question: Let the two base angles of a triangle be \(A\) and \(B,\) with \(B\) larger than \(A.\) The altitude to the base divides the vertex angle \(C\) into two parts, \(C_1\) and \(C_2,\) with \(C_2\) adjacent to side \(a.\) Then:
solution:
Use the usual convention that side \(a\) is opposite angle \(A\), so \(a=BC\). Interpret the stated division of the vertex angle as internal. Let \(D\) be the foot of the altitude from \(C\) to the base \(AB\); then \(D\) lies between \(A\) and \(B\).

Since \(C_2\) is adjacent to \(BC\), it is the angle at \(C\) in right triangle \(BCD\). The other part, \(C_1\), is the angle at \(C\) in right triangle \(ACD\). The acute angles in each right triangle are complementary, so
\[
C_1=90^\circ-A,
\qquad C_2=90^\circ-B.
\]
Subtracting removes the common \(90^\circ\):
\[
C_1-C_2=(90^\circ-A)-(90^\circ-B)=B-A.
\]
The answer is \(\mathrm{B}\).
